digest.intro: Referendums, fractals without computers, and surveillance going parabolic.

items.title: Iceland votes today on EU accession — split 46-46
items.source: International Centre for Defence and Security
items.blurb: Iceland is voting right now on whether to resume EU membership talks frozen since 2015 — and polls are essentially tied. What makes it bigger than 390,000 people: a yes sustains EU enlargement momentum at a fragile geopolitical moment, while a no hands ammunition to every Euroskeptic on the continent. Trump's Greenland saber-rattling has pushed Arctic security to the center of the debate in a way no one expected.

items.title: SpaceX acquired Cursor; OpenAI is cutting them off
items.blurb: OpenAI announced it's winding down its model contract with Cursor — now a SpaceX property — with a cutoff date of November 12, citing Musk's companies' documented pattern of contract violations, including an admission under oath that xAI violated OpenAI's terms of service. The letter is essentially a public paper trail being laid before any future litigation. The practical casualty is developer tooling: Cursor users lose OpenAI model access, and Astra (OpenAI's next model) will never ship through Cursor.

items.title: RFK lied to the Senate; 83 children died in Samoa
items.blurb: Newly released documents show RFK Jr. misrepresented his 2019 Samoa trip during confirmation hearings — a trip that preceded a measles outbreak that killed 83 people, mostly children under five, after vaccination rates cratered to 31%. Senator Wyden is calling for a DOJ criminal referral for lying to Congress. This has crossed from political scandal into documentary evidence of a specific, traceable public health harm.

items.title: Cities are dropping Flock surveillance contracts at three per day
items.blurb: 90 localities canceled Flock Safety license-plate-reader contracts in August alone — a fourfold spike over July, and 165 cancellations in just the first eight months of 2026. The reasons are a mix of cost, data-sharing overreach, and documented police abuse. Flock counters that new partnerships still outpace cancellations 10-to-1, but the advocacy group tracking this says the curve has "gone parabolic" and the dollar figures will start mattering soon.

sections.heading: Making things think, and things move

items.title: Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard: a USB moment for AI-to-device control
items.blurb: Anthropic's MHS is a standardized driver interface that lets AI agents talk to arbitrary physical hardware — microscopes, lasers, cameras — without bespoke translator code for every device pair. The inspiration was watching a neuroscientist spend months wiring together a memory-formation experiment at HHMI Janelia; MHS collapses that to hours. It's a research preview aimed at labs first, but the abstraction is obviously general — this is the layer that makes physical-world automation composable.

items.title: Curvature Béziers: making the curve that won't die actually better
items.blurb: Steven Wittens asks whether bézier curves — conceived in 1959, never dethroned despite decades of superior alternatives — can be improved without breaking the entire stack built on them. The answer is curvature béziers, a modification that preserves the lerp-based construction while giving designers control over curvature continuity that standard cubic béziers can't achieve. Every diagram in the post is interactive, and the writing is the rare kind that makes a math problem feel like an aesthetic argument.

items.title: The DSM is finally being rewritten around biology
items.blurb: An insider on the DSM's strategic committee explains how the next edition will introduce neurobiology into psychiatric diagnosis for the first time — carefully, using biological factors rather than hard biomarkers, because the science isn't settled enough to mandate measurable thresholds yet. The DSM-5 (2013) was criticized for medicalizing human suffering through symptom clusters with no objective biological grounding; the next edition attempts to thread between clinical usability and scientific validity. A genuine paradigm shift in how psychiatry defines what mental illness *is*.

items.title: Does the Sumerian King List encode actual climate events?
items.blurb: The antediluvian Sumerian kings supposedly ruled for tens of thousands of years — Alulim for 28,800, Enmenluana for 43,200 — numbers that are suspiciously precise multiples of 3,600 and 600. This interactive explorer rescales the entire 241,200-year sequence, anchors it to a proposed flood date, and overlays the resulting reign-boundary dates against a Quaternary paleoclimate event catalog to test whether the numbers might be garbled memory of real geological shifts. It's methodologically rigorous about what it isn't claiming, which makes the rabbit hole feel honest rather than crankish.

facts.fact: 90 cities dropped Flock Safety surveillance contracts in August 2026 alone — averaging three cancellations per day, a fourfold increase over the previous month.
Under oath earlier in 2026, Elon Musk admitted that xAI had violated OpenAI's terms of service — terms similar to xAI's own.
Samoa's measles vaccination rate fell to as low as 31% before a 2019 outbreak that killed 83 people, mostly children under five.
All eight antediluvian Sumerian kings' reign lengths are multiples of 600, and most are multiples of 3,600 — their total is exactly 241,200 years.
Iceland's 2026 referendum is its first-ever public vote on EU accession — a 2009 parliamentary proposal to hold such a referendum was defeated by a single abstention.

art_picks.title: La Jetée
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A 28-minute film made almost entirely of still photographs, it's a masterclass in how form can be the content — stillness as time, memory as loop, the archive as myth. If you work in generative systems and care about how brains construct reality, this one quietly restructures something in how you think about image-making.

art_picks.title: Obliteration Room
art_picks.creator: Yayoi Kusama
art_picks.why: A participatory installation where a white room is handed to visitors with dot stickers and collectively consumed — it's less about the dots and more about the feedback loop between individual mark-making and emergent pattern, which is exactly the physical/digital edge you live on.

art_picks.title: Music for 18 Musicians
art_picks.creator: Steve Reich
art_picks.why: The canonical example of systems thinking as composition — interlocking rhythmic cells that produce emergent, shimmering harmonics no individual performer could create alone. It's less 'music to listen to' and more a formal model for thinking about generative structures and the beauty inside constraint.

events.name: Iris van Herpen: Sculpting the Senses
events.why: 140+ haute couture pieces made via biomimicry, fractal geometry, and neuroscience — including a gown with 125 million living bioluminescent algae — shown alongside scientific specimens; it's less fashion show and more argument about where craft, code, and biology converge.

events.name: Arbrasson Workshop with Daniel Fishkin
events.venue: Pioneer Works, 159 Pioneer Street, Red Hook, Brooklyn
events.why: Fishkin builds custom instruments from unusual materials — the kind of obsessive, narrow-craft-meets-new-sound work that sits at the physical/digital edge and tends to make you want to go build something.

events.name: Camille Henrot: Dogs — Opening Celebration
events.venue: Doris C. Freedman Plaza, Central Park (5th Ave & 60th St), Manhattan
events.why: Henrot's first NYC public show deploys dog sculptures as a lens on domestication, societal rules, and the symbols we invent to create shared meaning — the exact intersection of banal surface and structural anthropology that makes her work worth your time.

events.name: Pioneer Works Fall 2026 Opening Reception (Siphon + Child/ren of the Bloom + There is no me without you)
events.venue: Pioneer Works, 159 Pioneer Street, Red Hook, Brooklyn
events.why: The anchor show Siphon — an 8K immersive video of octopus camouflage developed with a neuroscientist — is precisely the kind of work that lives at the edge where biology, perception, and image-making collapse into each other; the opening is free and public.
